title: Newer AI models missed more payment fraud in Coinbase’s benchmark
key_facts: Coinbase reported on 7 Oct 2026 that newer versions of three major AI model families caught fewer fraudulent payments, and a smaller share of fraud value, in a historical test of payment screening for its Onramp service, with an unchanged decision policy.
The replay covered 16,140 transactions across 7,293 users, including 813 confirmed fraudulent transactions, from the nine weeks before its risk agent rolled out.
Coinbase compared Opus 4.5 with Opus 5, Sonnet 4.6 with Sonnet 5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.6; every newer version had lower recall, lower F1 and lower dollar-weighted recall.
Sonnet's recall fell 22.2 percentage points and its dollar-weighted recall 22.9 points; Opus's recall fell 0.8 points; both newer models also had lower precision.
GPT's precision rose 11.5 points but its recall fell 20.7 points and dollar-weighted recall 21.8 points.
The replay does not establish customer losses from deploying those versions, and Coinbase said it could identify the regressions without establishing their cause.
In a separate 8 Oct 2026 disclosure, Coinbase said a post-trained Qwen3.5-9B model beat Opus 4.5 on four fraud-detection metrics and cut median LLM-request latency by 55%.
The SR-Fraud researchers say in their limitations that the proprietary dataset cannot be released, restricting independent replication.
quote_evidence: Every newer version had lower recall, a lower combined precision-and-recall score called F1, and lower dollar-weighted recall.
The replay does not establish customer losses from deploying those versions.
Coinbase also said it could identify the regressions without establishing their cause.
why_it_matters_hint: Upgrading an AI model does not automatically improve a payment-fraud screener, so firms need to test their own setup first.
